title: Solve it together: find the wrong approach
idea: GUIDED UEPCC with a wrong-approach focus. Print each temperature labelled hot/cold; spot and fix a flawed plan.
problem: For each temperature in a list, print 'hot' if it is above 30, otherwise 'cold'.

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: For each temperature, print 'hot' if above 30, else 'cold'.

What is the OUTPUT?
options: A single label for the list
exercises.explanation: One label per item — a per-item decision, not a single summary.

exercises.prompt: Example by hand. temps = [25, 35, 30]. What labels, in order?
exercises.explanation: 25 not above 30 -> cold; 35 above -> hot; 30 is NOT above 30 -> cold. Mind the edge at 30.

exercises.prompt: A temperature of exactly 30 is 'cold' here, because the rule says ABOVE 30 (strictly greater).
exercises.explanation: 'Above 30' means > 30, so 30 itself does not count as hot. Checking the edge by hand avoids a classic bug.

exercises.prompt: Plan: for each temp, decide hot/cold. Which tools?
exercises.explanation: Walk with for-each; choose with if/else so every item prints exactly one label.

exercises.prompt: A friend plans: 'check only the first temperature, then print one label for the whole list.' Why is that wrong?
options: It ignores the other temperatures — each needs its own label
exercises.explanation: The problem is per-item. Judging only the first temperature drops the rest — the wrong shape entirely.
'Above 30' is strictly greater: temp > 30. (>= would wrongly call 30 hot.)
Loop header, if (indent 1) + its print (indent 2), else (indent 1) + its print (indent 2).
else runs when the if is false, so every temperature gets exactly one label.

exercises.prompt: Check. Code on [25, 35, 30] prints cold, hot, cold. Hand example said cold, hot, cold. Verdict?
exercises.explanation: Matches, including the tricky 30 -> cold edge. Correct.
31 > 30 -> hot; 30 is not > 30 -> cold. The edge still behaves.
